q: Which is the most abundant type of cartilage in the human body?
x: Hyaline cartilage is the commonest type: it covers joint surfaces, forms the costal cartilages and supports the nose, trachea and bronchi. Elastic cartilage and fibrocartilage occur in far fewer places.

q: Elastic cartilage, rich in yellow elastic fibres, is found in the wall of the:
x: Elastic cartilage supports the pinna, the epiglottis and the Eustachian tube. The trachea has hyaline cartilage, while intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis contain fibrocartilage.

q: The crescent-shaped menisci that cushion the knee joint between the femur and the tibia are made of:
x: The menisci are fibrocartilage, whose thick collagen bundles resist pressure and absorb shock. Hyaline cartilage covers the bone ends but does not form the menisci.

q: The flexible cartilage that supports the tip of the nose and the walls of the bronchi is:
x: The nose, larynx (mostly), trachea and bronchi are supported by hyaline cartilage. Elastic cartilage is limited to places such as the pinna, epiglottis and Eustachian tube.

q: Inside the lacunae of cartilage, chondrocytes are usually seen:
o: In long rows of ten or more cells
Linked to each other by canaliculi
Singly or in small groups of two to four
Arranged in rings around a central canal
x: Chondrocytes lie in lacunae either singly or in small groups of two to four. Canaliculi and rings around a central canal are features of bone, not cartilage.

q: A student lists features of cartilage tissue. Which one is right?
o: Its matrix contains no blood vessels or nerves
Its matrix is hardened by calcium phosphate
Its cells are linked by canaliculi
Its matrix is arranged in Haversian systems
x: Cartilage is avascular and has no nerves; its cells get nutrients by diffusion through the matrix. Calcium phosphate hardening, canaliculi and Haversian systems all belong to bone.

q: The entire skeleton of a shark is made of:
x: Sharks belong to the cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes), whose skeleton is made entirely of cartilage. Chitin forms the exoskeleton of arthropods, not of fish.

q: In an adult long bone, the shaft (diaphysis) is made mainly of:
o: Hyaline cartilage with a thin bony covering
Compact bone surrounding a marrow cavity
x: The shaft is a tube of compact bone enclosing the marrow cavity. Spongy bone is mainly found in the enlarged ends (epiphyses).

q: The thin membrane that lines the marrow cavity of a long bone is the:
x: The endosteum lines the inner marrow cavity. The periosteum covers the outer surface of bone, and the perichondrium surrounds cartilage.

q: In compact bone, the Haversian canals run:
o: Parallel to the long axis of the bone
At right angles to the long axis of the bone
Only through the spongy ends of the bone
Only beneath the cartilage at joint surfaces
x: Haversian (central) canals run lengthwise, parallel to the long axis. The canals running across the bone at right angles are Volkmann's canals.

q: Within an osteon, the lacunae that contain osteocytes are located:
o: Between the concentric lamellae of matrix
x: Osteocytes sit in lacunae lying between the concentric rings (lamellae) of matrix around the Haversian canal. The canals themselves carry blood vessels and nerves.

q: The main role of osteocytes in mature bone is to:
x: Osteocytes are mature bone cells trapped in lacunae; they maintain the living bone matrix. Dissolving bone is the job of osteoclasts, and blood cells are made by red marrow.

q: Osteocytes need canaliculi to stay alive, but chondrocytes do not. The main reason is that:
o: Chondrocytes have their own blood capillaries
Cartilage matrix is full of blood vessels
Bone matrix is mineralised, so substances cannot diffuse easily through it
x: The hard, calcified matrix of bone blocks diffusion, so osteocytes rely on canaliculi to reach the blood supply. The softer cartilage matrix lets nutrients diffuse through it, even though cartilage has no blood vessels.

q: By weight, about what proportion of bone matrix is made of inorganic mineral salts?
x: Roughly two-thirds of bone matrix is inorganic (mainly calcium phosphate) and about one-third is organic (mainly collagen). One-third is the organic share, not the mineral share.

q: Spongy bone differs from compact bone in that spongy bone:
o: Has no mineral salts in its matrix
Is found only in the shaft of long bones
x: Spongy bone is a network of thin bony bars without osteons. It still has osteocytes and mineralised matrix, and it lies mainly in the ends of long bones, not the shaft.

q: Osteoclasts break down bone matrix by secreting:
o: Acid and enzymes that dissolve mineral and collagen
x: Osteoclasts release acid, which dissolves the mineral, and enzymes, which digest collagen. Secreting collagen and calcium salts is the work of osteoblasts.

q: The cytoplasm of a muscle fibre is called the:
x: Sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm of a muscle fibre. The sarcolemma is its cell membrane, a sarcomere is a contractile unit, and axoplasm is the cytoplasm of an axon.

q: A skeletal muscle fibre has many nuclei because, in the embryo, it is formed by:
o: Taking up nuclei from the nerves that supply it
Splitting of one large cell into many smaller ones
x: Each skeletal muscle fibre develops when many embryonic muscle-forming cells fuse end to end, so the fibre keeps all their nuclei. Nerves do not pass nuclei to muscle.

q: A whole skeletal muscle such as the biceps is made of bundles of muscle fibres. Each bundle is wrapped in:
x: Skeletal muscle fibres are grouped into bundles held together and wrapped by connective tissue, which also carries blood vessels and nerves and continues into the tendons.

q: The end of a skeletal muscle that is attached to a bone which stays fixed during contraction is called the muscle's:
x: The origin is the attachment to the bone that stays still. The insertion is the attachment to the bone that moves, and the belly is the thick, contracting middle part.

q: The biceps arises from the scapula and is inserted on the radius. When the biceps contracts:
o: The elbow straightens as the forearm is lowered
The scapula is pulled down towards the forearm
The elbow bends as the forearm is raised
x: A muscle pulls its insertion towards its origin. The biceps pulls the radius up towards the shoulder, so the elbow bends (flexion). Straightening the elbow is done by the triceps.

q: The biceps and triceps are called an antagonistic pair because they:
o: Always contract at the same time
Are made of different types of muscle
Produce opposite movements at the same joint
x: Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it. Both are skeletal muscles, and they contract alternately, not together.

q: A person straightens the arm at the elbow. Which statement is correct?
o: The biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes
The biceps pushes the forearm downwards
The triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes
x: Extension of the elbow is produced by contraction of the triceps, while its antagonist, the biceps, relaxes. Muscles cannot push; they only pull.

q: Tendons are well suited to joining muscle to bone because they are:
o: Highly elastic, so they stretch and absorb most of the pull
Made of hyaline cartilage, so they reduce friction
Strong and almost inelastic, so the pull of the muscle passes fully to the bone
Contractile, so they shorten together with the muscle
x: Tendons are dense bundles of collagen fibres: very strong and hardly stretchable, so the force of contraction is transmitted to the bone. They are not cartilage and cannot contract.

q: Which pairing of a supporting tissue with a component of its matrix is correct?
o: Bone – collagen fibres and calcium phosphate
Hyaline cartilage – thick bundles of yellow elastic fibres
Fibrocartilage – no fibres of any kind
x: Bone matrix combines collagen fibres with calcium phosphate. Elastic fibres are typical of elastic cartilage, fibrocartilage is rich in collagen bundles, and cartilage is not normally calcified.

q: A supporting tissue has cells in lacunae, a matrix full of thick collagen bundles and no perichondrium. It was most probably taken from the:
x: Thick collagen bundles and no perichondrium identify fibrocartilage, found in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs. The pinna and epiglottis are elastic cartilage and the nose is hyaline.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of cell found in bone?
x: Chondroblasts make cartilage. Bone contains osteoblasts (build matrix), osteocytes (maintain it) and osteoclasts (break it down).

q: Of the 206 bones of the adult human skeleton, the axial skeleton contains:
x: The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum, hyoid) has 80 bones. The remaining 126 make up the appendicular skeleton of the limbs and girdles.

q: The ribs that are joined directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages are the:
x: The first seven pairs are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage to the sternum. Pairs 8–10 join through the cartilage above, and pairs 11–12 are floating ribs with no front attachment.

q: The thoracic and lumbar regions of the human vertebral column contain, respectively:
x: There are 12 thoracic vertebrae, one for each pair of ribs, and 5 large lumbar vertebrae in the lower back. Seven is the number of cervical vertebrae.

q: The sacrum, which joins the vertebral column to the pelvic girdle, is formed by the fusion of:
x: The sacrum consists of five fused sacral vertebrae. It forms the back of the pelvis and articulates with the two hip bones.

q: The first cervical vertebra, which carries the skull and allows the nodding movement, is the:
x: The atlas (first cervical vertebra) supports the skull and lets the head nod. The axis is the second cervical vertebra, around which the atlas turns.

q: The head of the femur fits into a cup-shaped socket in the hip bone called the:
x: The acetabulum of the hip bone receives the head of the femur at the hip joint. The glenoid cavity of the scapula receives the humerus.

q: The large opening in the base of the skull through which the spinal cord passes is the:
x: The spinal cord leaves the cranium through the foramen magnum in the occipital bone. The obturator foramen is an opening in the hip bone.

q: Which bone of the lower leg carries most of the body's weight?
x: The tibia (shin bone) is the thick, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. The slender fibula mainly gives attachment to muscles, and the radius is in the forearm.

q: How many carpal bones are there in each human wrist?
x: Each wrist has eight small carpal bones. Seven is the number of tarsals in the ankle, five the number of metacarpals and fourteen the number of phalanges in a hand.

q: The number of phalanges in each human hand is:
x: The thumb has two phalanges and each of the other four fingers has three, giving 2 + 12 = 14.

q: The smallest bone in the human body, found in the middle ear, is the:
x: The stapes is the smallest bone. With the malleus and incus it passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

q: Which hormone raises the blood calcium level by stimulating osteoclasts to release calcium from bone?
x: Parathormone from the parathyroid glands increases bone resorption, releasing calcium into the blood. Calcitonin has the opposite effect.

q: Calcitonin lowers the blood calcium level mainly by:
o: Increasing calcium absorption from the intestine
Reducing bone resorption so that more calcium is deposited in bone
Releasing calcium stored in skeletal muscle
x: Calcitonin from the thyroid gland inhibits osteoclasts and favours deposition of calcium in bone, so blood calcium falls. Stimulating osteoclasts would raise blood calcium.

q: A child's diet lacks vitamin D for a long time. The bones become soft and the legs bow because:
o: No collagen can be made in the bones
Red marrow is replaced by yellow marrow
The cartilage at the joints becomes calcified
Too little calcium is absorbed to mineralise the bone matrix
x: Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium from the gut. Without it the bone matrix is poorly mineralised and stays soft (rickets), so weight-bearing bones bend.

q: Astronauts who spend months in weightlessness lose bone mass. The best explanation is that, without weight-bearing:
o: Osteoblasts become more active than osteoclasts
Bone marrow is converted into cartilage
Collagen in bone is replaced by elastic fibres
x: Bone is remodelled according to the loads it bears. With no weight on the skeleton, osteoclasts remove more bone than osteoblasts lay down, so bone density falls.

q: Growth in the length of a long bone stops when:
o: The epiphyseal (growth) plates are replaced by bone
Red marrow appears in the shaft
x: A long bone lengthens at its cartilage growth plates. At the end of puberty these plates ossify and fuse the ends to the shaft, so growth in length stops.

q: The sternum consists of three parts. These are the:
x: The sternum (breastbone) has an upper manubrium, a middle body and a lower xiphoid process. Ilium, ischium and pubis form the hip bone.

q: The female pelvis is broader and shallower than the male pelvis. This is an adaptation for:
x: The wider female pelvic opening allows the baby's head to pass during birth. It does not make running faster or protect the kidneys.

q: The cartilages of the larynx help mainly by:
o: Producing blood cells for the throat
Keeping the airway open and supporting the vocal cords
x: The firm but flexible laryngeal cartilages hold the airway open and support the vocal cords for voice production. Cartilage has no marrow, so it cannot make blood cells.

q: Bone is a living tissue, not just a dead mineral frame. Evidence for this is that bone:
o: Loses all its cells once the matrix is mineralised
Keeps the same matrix unchanged throughout life
Has blood vessels and nerves and can repair a fracture
Receives nutrients only by diffusion from cartilage
x: Bone is well supplied with blood vessels and nerves, its cells stay alive in lacunae, and it is constantly remodelled and can heal fractures.

q: A fracture through the growth plate of a 10-year-old's femur may leave that leg shorter. This is because the growth plate:
o: Is where the blood cells of the leg are made
Attaches the tendons to the bone
Stores calcium for the whole body
Is where new cartilage forms and is replaced by bone, lengthening the bone
x: Growth in length takes place at the epiphyseal plate, where cartilage keeps growing and is turned into bone. Damage there can stop this process, so the bone grows less than the other one.

q: Which feature lets bone, but not cartilage, bear heavy loads without bending?
o: A matrix hardened by calcium phosphate
x: Mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate, make bone matrix hard and rigid. Chondrin, elastic fibres and perichondrium are features of cartilage.

q: Which is a function of cartilage rather than of bone?
o: Giving flexible support that bends and springs back
Storing most of the body's calcium
Acting as rigid levers for movement
x: Cartilage gives firm but flexible support, as in the pinna and nose. Blood cell production, calcium storage and acting as levers are functions of bone.

q: The clavicle is commonly known as the:
x: The clavicle is the collar bone. The shoulder blade is the scapula, the breastbone is the sternum and the kneecap is the patella.

q: Which group contains ONLY bones of the appendicular skeleton?
o: Clavicle, femur, carpals and hip bones
x: The appendicular skeleton is the limbs plus the pectoral and pelvic girdles. The sternum, ribs and hyoid are all axial, so each wrong group contains one axial bone.

q: In a young child, red bone marrow is found in:
o: Nearly all bones, including the shafts of long bones
Only the flat bones such as the ribs and sternum
Only the ends of the femur
x: In young children almost every bone, including long-bone shafts, holds red marrow. Later the shafts fill with yellow marrow and red marrow becomes limited mainly to flat bones and the ends of long bones.

q: If all the parathyroid glands were removed, the most direct effect on calcium would be:
o: A rise in blood calcium, because bone is dissolved faster
A fall in blood calcium, because less calcium is released from bone
Faster growth of the epiphyseal plates
Softening of all the body's cartilage
x: Parathormone normally stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone. Without it, less calcium leaves the bone and blood calcium falls.

q: The muscle in the walls of arteries that narrows them during vasoconstriction is:
x: The middle layer of an artery wall contains smooth muscle, which contracts involuntarily to narrow the vessel. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.

q: The tiny arrector pili muscles that make the hairs of the skin stand up are made of:
x: Arrector pili muscles are small bundles of involuntary smooth muscle attached to hair follicles. We cannot raise our hairs at will.

q: During an asthma attack, the airways narrow because of contraction of:
o: Smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchioles
x: The bronchioles have smooth muscle in their walls; its contraction narrows the airways. The diaphragm and intercostals are skeletal breathing muscles that do not line the airways.

q: The muscles that move the eyeball in different directions are:
o: The same muscles that control the pupil
x: The muscles attached to the outside of the eyeball are skeletal and under voluntary control. The muscles of the iris, which change pupil size, are smooth.

q: The sinoatrial (SA) node, the pacemaker of the heart, is made of:
o: Nerve cells of the vagus nerve
x: The SA node is a patch of modified cardiac muscle that starts each heartbeat on its own. Nerves such as the vagus only change the rate.

q: Which order ranks the three muscle types from the FASTEST to the SLOWEST speed of contraction?
x: Skeletal muscle contracts fastest, cardiac muscle at an intermediate speed, and smooth muscle slowest, though smooth muscle can stay contracted for a long time.

q: Cardiac muscle cells contain very many mitochondria. This suits them because they:
o: Respire mainly anaerobically to make lactic acid
Contract continuously and depend on aerobic respiration
x: The heart beats throughout life without rest, so its cells need a steady supply of ATP from aerobic respiration in mitochondria.

q: Which type of muscle has the longest cells, some running for several centimetres?
o: All three have cells of the same length
x: Skeletal muscle fibres are long multinucleate cells that may run much of the length of a muscle. Smooth muscle cells are short spindles, and cardiac cells are short and branched.

q: Which feature is found in smooth muscle but NOT in skeletal muscle?
x: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, tapering at both ends. Striations, many nuclei and somatic nerve control are features of skeletal muscle.

q: Which feature is shared by all three types of muscle?
o: Contraction depends on actin and myosin filaments
x: Smooth, cardiac and skeletal muscle all contract by the interaction of actin and myosin. Smooth muscle lacks striations, only cardiac has intercalated discs, and only skeletal is voluntary.

q: Which description fits cardiac muscle but not skeletal muscle?
o: Branched cells joined end to end by intercalated discs
x: Branching and intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle. Striations, sarcomeres and plentiful mitochondria are present in skeletal muscle as well.

q: The stomach wall stretches greatly after a meal and then contracts slowly to churn the food. Its muscle layers are:
x: The wall of the stomach contains layers of smooth muscle, which can be stretched a lot and contract slowly and involuntarily to mix food.

q: Adrenaline released during fright speeds up the heart and also widens the pupils. Which muscle types does it act on here?
x: The heart wall is cardiac muscle, and the pupil is widened by smooth muscle of the iris. Neither effect involves skeletal muscle.

q: The muscles of facial expression, used in smiling, are:
x: We smile at will, so facial muscles are voluntary skeletal muscles. Involuntary striated muscle describes cardiac muscle.

q: Cardiac muscle is described as striated. This means it:
o: Shows alternating light and dark bands
Has only one nucleus in each cell
x: Striated means cross-banded: light and dark bands produced by the regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments. Branching and single nuclei are separate features.

q: During long, continuous activity, which type of muscle tires (fatigues) most quickly?
o: All three tire at the same rate
x: Skeletal muscle contracts quickly and powerfully but fatigues fast. Cardiac muscle works throughout life without fatigue, and smooth muscle can keep a slow contraction for a long time.

q: Which statement about the control of muscles is correct?
o: Cardiac muscle contracts only when stimulated by voluntary nerves
Smooth muscle is controlled by the somatic nervous system
Skeletal muscle is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
Skeletal muscle contracts only when stimulated by somatic motor nerves, but cardiac muscle beats on its own
x: Skeletal muscle needs impulses from somatic motor neurons. Cardiac muscle is myogenic, and both cardiac and smooth muscle are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.

q: Waves of contraction in the ureters, which push urine from the kidneys to the bladder, are produced by:
x: Peristalsis in the ureters is produced by smooth muscle in their walls, working involuntarily.

q: The nuclei of skeletal muscle fibres lie at the edge of the fibre. In a cardiac muscle cell, the nucleus lies:
o: Near the centre of the cell
At both ends of the cell
x: Cardiac muscle cells have one (sometimes two) centrally placed nuclei, unlike the many peripheral nuclei of skeletal fibres.

q: A drug that relaxes smooth muscle would most directly help to:
o: Ease painful spasms of the intestinal wall
Increase the strength of the biceps
x: The intestinal wall is smooth muscle, so relaxing smooth muscle eases its spasms. The heart is cardiac muscle and the biceps and leg muscles are skeletal.

q: Which list contains ONLY involuntary muscles?
o: Eyeball muscles, stomach wall, heart wall
x: Cardiac muscle of the heart and smooth muscle of the iris and stomach are all involuntary. The diaphragm, tongue, biceps and eyeball muscles are skeletal (voluntary).

q: Smooth muscle is also known as:
x: Smooth muscle shows no cross-striations, so it is called unstriated (non-striated) muscle. It is also involuntary.

q: A property of cardiac muscle that skeletal muscle lacks is that cardiac muscle:
o: Contracts rhythmically on its own, without a nerve impulse
Is attached to bones by tendons
x: Cardiac muscle is myogenic: the heartbeat starts within the muscle itself. Skeletal muscle contracts only when a motor nerve stimulates it. Both contain actin and myosin and are striated.

q: Artery walls contain smooth muscle rather than skeletal muscle. An advantage of this is that the muscle:
o: Can stay contracted for long periods without tiring or conscious effort
Contracts faster than any other muscle
x: Vessel diameter must be adjusted all day without our thinking about it. Smooth muscle is involuntary and keeps up slow, sustained contraction without fatigue. All muscle needs ATP.

q: Which comparison of skeletal and smooth muscle is correct?
o: Skeletal fibres are multinucleate; smooth muscle cells have one nucleus
Skeletal muscle is involuntary; smooth muscle is voluntary
Smooth muscle is striated; skeletal muscle is not
x: Skeletal fibres have many nuclei, while each smooth muscle cell has a single central nucleus. Neither is branched, skeletal is voluntary, and only skeletal is striated.

q: Which pair of features would be seen in the muscle of the small intestine wall but NOT in the biceps?
x: The intestinal wall is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, unstriated cells. Striations, many peripheral nuclei and sarcomeres belong to the biceps; intercalated discs are found only in the heart.

q: The fluid matrix that surrounds the myofibrils, mitochondria and glycogen granules inside a muscle cell is named:
x: The cytoplasm of a muscle fibre is the sarcoplasm; it holds the myofibrils, mitochondria and glycogen. The sarcolemma is the cell membrane, and the sarcomere is the contractile unit of a myofibril.

q: How are myofibrils oriented inside a long striated muscle cell?
o: At right angles to the long axis of the fibre
In a random network through the sarcoplasm
In a spiral around the nuclei
Parallel to the long axis of the fibre
x: Myofibrils lie side by side along the length of the fibre. Because they run parallel to the long axis, their shortening shortens the whole fibre.

q: The A band and I band of a sarcomere are named after how they affect polarised light. The letters stand for:
x: The dark A band is anisotropic (it bends polarised light) and the light I band is isotropic. The names have nothing to do with actin or with activity.

q: The M line runs across the middle of which band of a sarcomere?
o: Overlap zone of the I band
x: The M line lies at the centre of the A band, inside the H zone, where it holds the thick filaments together. The Z line, not the M line, lies in the middle of the I band.

q: In a relaxed sarcomere, the paler region seen at the centre of the dark A band is the:
x: The H zone is the central part of the A band that thin filaments do not reach in a relaxed sarcomere, so it looks paler than the overlap regions beside it. The I band lies outside the A band.

q: In a thin filament of skeletal muscle, the long thread-like tropomyosin molecules lie:
o: Inside the hollow core of the thick filament
Across the Z line, joining two sarcomeres
Within the membrane of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Along the grooves of the twisted actin chains
x: Tropomyosin is a long fibrous protein that lies in the grooves of the actin double helix. In this position it can cover the myosin-binding sites on actin.

q: Within a thin filament, troponin molecules are found:
o: Only at the M line in the centre of the sarcomere
On the heads of the myosin molecules
Attached to tropomyosin at regular intervals along the filament
Free in the sarcoplasm between myofibrils
x: Troponin is a small protein complex bound to tropomyosin at regular intervals along the thin filament. It is part of the thin filament, not of myosin, and it is not free in the sarcoplasm.

q: Which structure is NOT found in a skeletal muscle fibre?
x: Intercalated discs join neighbouring cardiac muscle cells and are absent from skeletal muscle. Skeletal fibres do have sarcoplasmic reticulum, T-tubules and Z lines.

q: The sarcoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fibre is a specialised form of the:
x: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a modified smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a network of membrane sacs and tubes around each myofibril. It carries no ribosomes and is not part of the Golgi apparatus.

q: Each Z line of a myofibril anchors thin filaments belonging to:
o: The thick filaments of the same sarcomere
Myofibrils of a neighbouring muscle fibre
x: A Z line is the boundary shared by two sarcomeres, so thin filaments project from it into the sarcomere on each side. Thick filaments are not attached to the Z line; they are held at the M line.

q: Which property of the sarcolemma lets a skeletal muscle fibre respond to its motor neuron?
o: It is fully permeable to every ion
It contains the contractile proteins actin and myosin
It stores calcium ions inside its folds
It is excitable and can conduct an action potential
x: Like a neuron's membrane, the sarcolemma is excitable: it can depolarise and carry an action potential over the fibre and into the T-tubules. Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in the sarcolemma.

q: Each skeletal muscle fibre contains many nuclei because it:
o: Divides its nucleus repeatedly without ever forming fibres
Takes up nuclei from nearby nerve cells
Is made of many cells joined by intercalated discs
Forms by the fusion of many embryonic cells (myoblasts)
x: During development many myoblasts fuse to form one long fibre, so the fibre ends up with many nuclei. Intercalated discs belong to cardiac muscle, whose cells stay separate.

q: Which statement about the thick filaments of a relaxed sarcomere is correct?
o: They lie in the A band and do not reach the Z lines
They extend all the way from one Z line to the next
They are found only in the I band
They are attached at both ends to the Z lines
x: Thick (myosin) filaments occupy the A band and are held at their centres by the M line; their ends stop short of the Z lines. The I band contains thin filaments only.

q: In a relaxed sarcomere, each thin filament runs from:
o: The M line to the Z line on the same side
One Z line to the next Z line
A Z line partway into the A band
The H zone to the M line
x: Thin filaments are anchored at the Z line and extend through the I band into the outer part of the A band, overlapping the thick filaments. In a relaxed sarcomere they do not reach the H zone or the M line.

q: The length of the A band of a sarcomere is always equal to the length of:
o: Two thin filaments placed end to end
The I band plus the H zone
x: The A band is defined by the thick filaments, so its length equals the length of a thick filament. That is why the A band stays the same length whether the sarcomere is relaxed or contracted.

q: A relaxed sarcomere is 2.5 µm long. Each thin filament extends 1.0 µm from its Z line. How wide is the H zone?
x: The H zone is the central gap between the tips of the thin filaments from the two Z lines: 2.5 − (1.0 + 1.0) = 0.5 µm. The value 1.5 µm comes from wrongly subtracting only one thin filament.

q: A myofibril is 1 cm long and each of its sarcomeres is 2.5 µm long. About how many sarcomeres lie end to end in it?
x: 1 cm = 10 000 µm, and 10 000 ÷ 2.5 = 4000 sarcomeres. Errors in converting centimetres to micrometres give 400 or 40 000.

q: A cross-section through the overlap region of the A band shows each thick filament surrounded by:
o: Six thin filaments in a hexagonal pattern
Two thin filaments, one on each side
Twelve thick filaments in a ring
x: Where thick and thin filaments overlap, each thick filament is surrounded by six thin filaments arranged in a hexagon. This allows its myosin heads to reach thin filaments on all sides.

q: In each half of a thick filament, the myosin molecules are arranged with:
o: Heads pointing toward the M line and tails toward the Z line
All heads gathered at the M line
Tails pointing toward the M line and heads pointing toward the Z line
Heads and tails lying in a random mix
x: Myosin tails are bundled toward the centre (M line) and the heads project outward toward the Z lines. So the heads in each half pull the thin filaments of that half toward the centre.

q: The glycogen granules found in the sarcoplasm of skeletal muscle fibres serve as:
o: Binding sites for calcium ions during contraction
The protein that forms the thick filaments
A store of fuel that can be broken down to make ATP
x: Glycogen is stored carbohydrate; it is broken down to glucose, which is respired to make ATP for contraction. Calcium is bound by troponin, and acetylcholine receptors lie on the sarcolemma.

q: According to the sliding filament theory, when a sarcomere contracts the actin and myosin filaments themselves:
x: The filaments do not shorten; they slide past one another so that their overlap increases. The sarcomere shortens even though each filament keeps its length.

q: The sliding filament theory of muscle contraction was put forward in 1954 by:
x: Hugh Huxley and Jean Hanson proposed the sliding filament model in 1954 from studies of muscle bands. Watson and Crick described DNA structure, and Schleiden and Schwann the cell theory.

q: The stored carbohydrate broken down in skeletal muscle to provide glucose for making ATP during exercise is:
x: Muscle stores carbohydrate as glycogen, which is broken down to glucose for respiration. Starch and cellulose are plant polysaccharides, and sucrose is a plant sugar.

q: As a skeletal muscle fibre contracts, the region where thick and thin filaments overlap:
x: Thin filaments slide further in between the thick filaments, so the overlap region grows while the I band and H zone shrink. It is the H zone, not the overlap, that can disappear.

q: As a myosin head swings and pulls actin in the power stroke, which molecules leave it?
x: ADP and phosphate are released as the head swivels in the power stroke. A new ATP then binds to detach the head; calcium stays with troponin, and acetylcholine acts only at the sarcolemma.

q: One cross-bridge cycle moves a thin filament only a very short distance. A sarcomere can still shorten a lot because:
o: Each power stroke breaks the thin filament into pieces
The thick filaments shorten after each stroke
The Z lines move apart between strokes
Each myosin head attaches, pulls and detaches many times
x: Many myosin heads cycle repeatedly, each time attaching further along the actin, like hands pulling a rope. The filaments do not shorten or break, and the Z lines move closer together, not apart.

q: The specialised region of the sarcolemma lying under the axon terminal of a motor neuron, carrying acetylcholine receptors, is the:
x: The motor end plate is the folded part of the muscle fibre membrane at the neuromuscular junction, rich in acetylcholine receptors. The synaptic knob belongs to the neuron, and nodes of Ranvier lie along myelinated axons.

q: Which is the correct order of events in one cross-bridge cycle?
o: ATP binds → head attaches to actin → ATP split → power stroke
Power stroke → head attaches to actin → ATP split → ATP binds
Head attaches to actin → power stroke → ATP binds and head detaches → ATP split, head re-cocked
Head detaches → power stroke → head attaches → ATP binds
x: The energised head binds actin, swings in the power stroke, then a new ATP binds and releases it; splitting that ATP re-cocks the head for the next cycle. The power stroke cannot happen before the head is attached.

q: When the calcium concentration in the sarcoplasm falls after stimulation stops, contraction ends because:
o: Myosin heads lose their ATPase activity permanently
Actin filaments break away from the Z lines
Calcium leaves troponin and tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin again
x: Without calcium bound, troponin lets tropomyosin slip back over the myosin-binding sites, so no new cross-bridges can form. The proteins are not damaged and the filaments stay attached to the Z lines.

q: Lactic acid formed in skeletal muscle during vigorous exercise is mostly carried by the blood to the:
o: Liver, where it is converted back to pyruvate or glucose
Lungs, where it is breathed out
x: The liver takes up lactic acid and turns it back into pyruvate and glucose, using oxygen taken in during recovery. Lactic acid is not exhaled and is not stored in the spleen.

q: Compared with aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration in a working muscle:
o: Gives far more ATP molecules per glucose
Gives far fewer ATP molecules per glucose
x: Anaerobic respiration stops at lactic acid and yields only 2 ATP per glucose, far fewer than complete aerobic oxidation. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are made by yeast, not by human muscle.

q: A drug stops the calcium pumps of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, while ATP supply stays normal. After one stimulus the muscle fibre will most directly:
o: Stay contracted, because calcium remains in the sarcoplasm
Fail to contract at all, because no calcium is released
Lose its ability to make acetylcholine
x: Calcium is still released on stimulation, so the fibre contracts, but it cannot be pumped back. With calcium left on troponin, the binding sites stay exposed and relaxation fails.

q: The term 'excitation–contraction coupling' refers to:
o: The joining of two muscles in an antagonistic pair
The binding of ATP to the myosin head
The link by which an action potential on the sarcolemma causes calcium release inside the fibre
The fusion of myoblasts to form a muscle fibre
x: Excitation (the action potential) is coupled to contraction when the impulse travels down the T-tubules and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The other options are separate processes.

q: Skeletal muscles that move a bone usually work in antagonistic pairs because a muscle:
o: Can only pull when it contracts and cannot push
Can contract only once and then must be replaced
Pushes the bone when it relaxes
Needs a second muscle to supply its ATP
x: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls; it cannot actively push. So a second muscle on the other side of the joint is needed to pull the bone back.

q: When the elbow is bent (flexed) to lift the forearm:
o: The biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes
The triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes
Both biceps and triceps contract fully
Both biceps and triceps relax fully
x: The biceps is the flexor of the elbow; it contracts and pulls the forearm up while its antagonist, the triceps, relaxes. The triceps contracts to straighten (extend) the arm.

q: A whole myofibril shortens noticeably during contraction because:
o: Only the sarcomere at one end shortens greatly
All the sarcomeres along it shorten at the same time
Its thick filaments fold in half
New sarcomeres are removed during contraction
x: A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres, and they all shorten together, so their small changes add up to a large shortening. Filaments do not fold and sarcomeres are not removed.

q: Which distance in a sarcomere stays the same during contraction?
o: From one Z line to the next Z line
From a Z line to the nearest edge of the A band
From the M line to the tip of a thick filament
Across the width of the H zone
x: The M line to the tip of a thick filament is half the A band, and it stays constant because thick filaments do not shorten. Z line to Z line, the half I band and the H zone all shrink as thin filaments slide in.

q: Thick filaments are 1.6 µm and each thin filament 1.0 µm long. A sarcomere is stretched to 3.8 µm and then stimulated. It will:
o: Produce no force, because thick and thin filaments no longer overlap
Produce its greatest force, because the H zone is widest
Shorten normally, because calcium is still released
Produce force only by shortening its thick filaments
x: Thin filaments reach 1.0 µm in from each Z line, but the thick filaments start (3.8 − 1.6) ÷ 2 = 1.1 µm in, so there is no overlap. Without overlap no cross-bridges can form, even though calcium is released.

q: A myofibril has 1000 sarcomeres in series. Each shortens from 2.5 µm to 2.0 µm. By how much does the myofibril shorten?
x: Each sarcomere shortens by 0.5 µm, so the total is 1000 × 0.5 µm = 500 µm = 0.5 mm. The answer 0.5 µm is the change in a single sarcomere only.

q: A sarcomere is 2.4 µm long and its H zone is 0.4 µm wide. Assuming the thin filaments from both Z lines are equal, how long is each thin filament?
x: The two thin filaments together cover the sarcomere except the H zone: 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 µm, so each is 1.0 µm. The value 2.0 µm forgets to divide between the two sides.

q: Grouping joints as immovable, slightly movable and freely movable is a classification based on:
o: The size of the bones that meet
The number of bones in the joint
The amount of movement they allow
x: This is the functional classification of joints, by degree of movement. It matches the structural types: fibrous joints are immovable, cartilaginous slightly movable and synovial freely movable.

q: A tendon attaches:
x: Tendons connect muscles to bones and transmit the pull of the muscle to the skeleton. Ligaments are the bands that join bone to bone at a joint.

q: The movements possible at a hinge joint are:
o: Rotation around the long axis only
Bending and straightening (flexion and extension) in one plane
x: A hinge joint works like a door hinge: it bends and straightens in one plane only. Rotation is the movement of a pivot joint, and movement in all directions belongs to a ball-and-socket joint.

q: The joints between the tarsal bones of the ankle region, which let flat bone surfaces slide slightly over each other, are:
x: Like the joints between carpal bones, intertarsal joints have flat surfaces that slide a little over one another, which makes them gliding (plane) joints.

q: The knuckle joints, between the metacarpals and the first phalanges of the fingers, are:
x: At the knuckles, the rounded head of a metacarpal fits an oval hollow on the phalanx, allowing bending and side-to-side movement: a condyloid joint. The joints between the phalanges themselves are hinge joints.

q: In the hip joint, the head of the femur fits into the:
x: The acetabulum is the deep cup-shaped socket of the hip bone that holds the head of the femur. The glenoid cavity is the shoulder's socket, and the obturator foramen is an opening, not a socket.

q: In the shoulder joint, the head of the humerus fits into the:
x: The shoulder's socket is the shallow glenoid cavity on the scapula. The acetabulum is the hip socket, and the olecranon is part of the ulna at the elbow.

q: Which bone does NOT take part in forming the knee joint?
x: The knee joint is formed by the femur, the tibia and the patella (kneecap). The fibula lies alongside the tibia but does not reach the knee joint itself.

q: Both the shoulder and the hip are ball-and-socket joints, yet the hip is more stable. This is mainly because the hip has:
o: A shallow socket that allows more movement
Fibrous tissue in place of synovial fluid
A deep socket that holds the femur's head firmly
x: The deep acetabulum and strong ligaments hold the femur securely, giving stability for weight bearing. The shoulder's shallow glenoid cavity allows more movement but dislocates more easily.

q: Swinging the arm round in a full circle (circumduction) is possible at the shoulder because it is a:
x: A ball-and-socket joint allows movement in all planes, so the limb can trace a circle. Hinge joints move in one plane, pivot joints only rotate, and gliding joints only slide.

q: In a newborn baby, the soft spots (fontanelles) between the skull bones are:
o: Synovial joints that remain freely movable for life
Cartilaginous discs like those between vertebrae
Membrane-covered gaps that later close into immovable sutures
Gliding joints that allow the bones to slide freely
x: Fontanelles are areas of fibrous membrane between the growing skull bones. As the bones grow they close, and the bones are then joined by fibrous, immovable sutures.

q: The joint between the lower jaw (mandible) and the skull, which moves during chewing and speaking, is a:
x: The jaw joint moves freely and has a fluid-filled cavity, so it is a synovial joint. The other skull bones are joined by immovable fibrous sutures.

q: The small joints between the articular processes of neighbouring vertebrae, where flat surfaces slide on each other, are:
x: These joints have flat facing surfaces that slide a little, so they are gliding (plane) synovial joints. The vertebral bodies themselves are joined by cartilaginous intervertebral discs.

q: Each joint between vertebral bodies allows only slight movement, yet the backbone as a whole can bend a lot. This is because:
o: Each vertebra can rotate freely like a pivot
The intervertebral discs are synovial cavities
Small movements at many joints add up
The vertebrae are not connected to one another
x: The vertebral column has many slightly movable joints in a row, and their small movements add together to give a large bend. The discs are cartilage, not synovial cavities.

q: A student lists features of freely movable joints. Which item on the list is NOT correct?
o: They join the flat bones of the adult skull
They have a cavity containing synovial fluid
Their bone ends are covered with articular cartilage
They are enclosed by a joint capsule
x: The flat bones of the adult skull are joined by fibrous sutures, not synovial joints. A cavity with fluid, articular cartilage and a capsule are all features of synovial joints.

q: The largest synovial joint of the human body is the:
x: The knee, between the femur, tibia and patella, is the largest synovial joint in the body. The elbow, wrist and ankle are all much smaller.

q: The elbow joint is formed where the lower end of the humerus meets the upper ends of the:
x: At the elbow the humerus meets the ulna (the main hinge) and the radius. Tibia and fibula are leg bones, and scapula and clavicle form the shoulder girdle.

q: Which pair contains only joints that allow movement around a single axis?
x: A hinge bends in one plane and a pivot rotates around one axis, so both are single-axis joints. Saddle and condyloid joints move in two planes, and ball-and-socket joints in all planes.

q: An oval, rounded bone end fits into an oval hollow. The joint bends forward and backward and side to side, but cannot rotate. This joint is a:
x: An oval surface in an oval hollow gives movement in two planes without rotation: a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint. A ball-and-socket joint would also allow rotation, and a pivot allows rotation only.

q: An X-ray of a 10-year-old shows a plate of hyaline cartilage joining the shaft of a long bone to its end. This is a temporary joint of which type?
x: The growth (epiphyseal) plate joins two parts of a bone by cartilage with no cavity, so it is a cartilaginous joint; it turns to bone when growth ends. It has no synovial fluid and no fibrous tissue joining the parts.

q: In the word 'arthritis', the ending '-itis' means:
x: 'Arthr-' means joint and '-itis' means inflammation, so arthritis is inflammation of a joint. The same ending is used in words such as tonsillitis and hepatitis.

q: The most common form of arthritis is:
x: Osteoarthritis, linked to wear of joint cartilage with age, is by far the most common form. Rheumatoid arthritis, gout and infective arthritis are less common.

q: Unlike osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis may also cause:
o: Bony spurs as its main feature
General symptoms such as tiredness and mild fever
Damage limited to one weight-bearing joint
Urate crystals in the joint fluid
x: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease of the whole body, so it can bring tiredness and fever as well as joint pain. Bony spurs belong to osteoarthritis and urate crystals to gout.

q: Which of the following increases the risk of an attack of gout?
o: Eating a diet low in purines
x: Alcohol, especially beer, raises blood uric acid and can trigger gout attacks. Plenty of water helps the kidneys remove uric acid, and a low-purine diet lowers it.

q: Septic (infective) arthritis is caused by:
o: The immune system attacking the joint lining
Infection of a joint by microorganisms such as bacteria
x: Septic arthritis is inflammation of a joint due to infection, usually by bacteria. Urate crystals cause gout, autoimmunity causes rheumatoid arthritis, and wear causes osteoarthritis.

q: A student claims arthritis affects only elderly people. The correct reply is that arthritis:
o: Affects only the joints of the hands
Can occur at any age, including in children
x: Although osteoarthritis is common in older people, forms of arthritis can affect any age, including children. It may involve many different joints and has several causes, not only infection.

q: Rheumatoid arthritis is called an autoimmune disease. This means that:
o: It is caused by a virus that attacks immune cells
The body's immune system attacks its own tissues
It spreads from person to person by contact
The joints lose all their immune cells
x: In an autoimmune disease the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue; in rheumatoid arthritis this is mainly the synovial membrane. It is not infectious and is not caused by loss of immune cells.

q: In a person with gout, uric acid may also form deposits outside the joints, for example as:
x: Uric acid is excreted by the kidneys, and at high levels it can crystallise there to form kidney stones. Arterial plaques and gallstones have other causes.

q: A footballer had a serious knee injury, with torn cartilage, several years ago. In later life that knee is at higher risk of:
x: Damage to a joint's cartilage speeds up its wear, so an old injury is a known risk factor for osteoarthritis in that joint. Gout and rheumatoid arthritis are caused by uric acid and autoimmunity, not injury.

q: Which pairing of a form of arthritis with its main cause is correct?
o: Osteoarthritis — immune attack on the joint lining
Rheumatoid arthritis — high uric acid in the blood
Gout — deposition of urate crystals in joints
Septic arthritis — gradual wear of cartilage with age
x: Gout is caused by urate crystal deposition. Immune attack is the cause of rheumatoid arthritis, wear with age of osteoarthritis, and infection of septic arthritis.

q: The swelling of a joint affected by arthritis is partly due to:
o: The bones of the joint growing longer
Extra fluid collecting in the joint cavity
Loss of all the synovial fluid
x: Inflammation makes the synovial membrane produce extra fluid, which collects in the joint and makes it swell. Bones do not lengthen, and losing fluid would not cause swelling.

q: The pattern of gout over time is typically:
o: Slow, steady worsening over decades with no flares
Constant mild pain from childhood onward
Sudden painful attacks separated by periods with no symptoms
A single attack that never returns
x: Gout usually comes as sudden flares lasting days, with symptom-free gaps between attacks. Slow, steady worsening over many years is the pattern of osteoarthritis.

q: How does osteoarthritis typically develop over time?
o: Suddenly overnight after a heavy meal
Within days after bacteria enter the joint
Mainly in early childhood, then disappears
x: Osteoarthritis develops gradually as joint cartilage wears down over years. A sudden attack after a heavy meal suggests gout, and bacterial infection causes septic arthritis.

q: A patient's joint pain gets worse with use during the day and eases with rest; morning stiffness lasts only a few minutes. This pattern points most to:
x: Pain that builds with use and settles with rest, with brief morning stiffness, is typical of osteoarthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis gives long morning stiffness that eases with movement, and gout and septic arthritis come on suddenly.

q: Why do crystals form in the joints in gout?
o: Uric acid is poorly soluble, so at high levels it comes out of solution
Calcium is drawn out of the bones into the joint fluid
Synovial fluid freezes in cold joints
x: Uric acid dissolves poorly in body fluids; when its level rises too high it crystallises as needle-shaped urate crystals in joints. The crystals are not calcium or cartilage fragments.

q: Which form of arthritis results from a metabolic disorder, rather than from wear or from an immune attack?
x: Gout comes from a disorder of uric acid metabolism, leading to high blood uric acid. Osteoarthritis is degenerative wear, and rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune.

q: A man's blood test shows a raised uric acid level, but he has never had joint pain. Which statement is correct?
o: He must already have advanced osteoarthritis
Gout arises only when urate crystals deposit in joints, so a high level alone may cause no symptoms
He has rheumatoid arthritis, because uric acid attacks the synovial membrane
A raised uric acid level always causes immediate joint pain
x: Gout attacks happen when urate crystals are deposited in a joint and inflame it; a raised level without crystals can be symptom-free. Raised uric acid is not a sign of osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.

q: Arthritis differs from a sprain because arthritis is:
o: A torn ligament, while a sprain is inflammation of cartilage
Inflammation of the joint itself, while a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament
A broken bone near a joint, while a sprain is a muscle cramp
Always caused by injury, while a sprain has no cause
x: Arthritis is inflammation of a joint, from causes such as wear, autoimmunity or crystals. A sprain is an injury in which a ligament is stretched or torn.

q: If gout attacks keep returning over many years without control, a likely long-term result is:
o: Complete regrowth of the joint cartilage
Damage and deformity of the affected joints
Permanent loss of all uric acid from the blood
x: Repeated inflammation from urate crystals gradually damages cartilage and bone, so the joints can become deformed. Cartilage does not regrow, and uric acid does not disappear from the blood.
